q: What is the difference between the Internet and the World Wide Web?
options: They are two names for the same thing
The Internet is the network infrastructure; the Web is one service running on it
The Web is the hardware; the Internet is the software
The Internet is only for email; the Web is for pages
why: The Internet is a network of networks (infrastructure plus TCP/IP). The Web is one service on it: HTML pages joined by links and delivered by HTTP.

q: Which of these uses the Internet but is NOT part of the Web?
options: A news article you open in Chrome
why: Email, games, streaming and WhatsApp all travel over the Internet, but they are not HTML pages delivered over HTTP, so they are not the Web.

q: In the client-server model, which side displays the page?
options: The browser, which is the client
why: The browser is the client: it requests and displays. The server stores data, runs logic and responds.

q: HTML, CSS and JavaScript are responsible for, in order:
why: HTML is structure, CSS is presentation, JavaScript is behaviour.

q: Why is HTML called a markup language rather than a programming language?
options: It runs slower than a programming language
It labels what content is, rather than computing or deciding anything
It cannot be written by hand
why: HTML marks up content to say what it is. It has no logic, variables or decisions, so it is a markup language, not a programming language.

q: Which body publishes the open standards of the web, including WCAG?
why: The W3C (World Wide Web Consortium) publishes the open web standards and WCAG; WHATWG maintains the HTML living standard and MDN documents them.

q: A student says 'I hid the answer key in the HTML, so students cannot see it.' What is wrong?
options: The response is text the browser interprets, so nothing sent to a browser is secret
why: The server's response is text which the browser interprets. Anything sent to a browser can be read, so nothing sent to a browser is secret.

q: What does it mean that HTTP is stateless?
options: The server does not remember you between requests
It works only once per session
why: HTTP is stateless: the server does not remember you between requests, which is why cookies exist to do the remembering.

q: In https://portal.lpu.in/results/view.html?reg=12345, what is '?reg=12345'?
why: A URL is protocol :// domain / path ? query string. Everything after ? is the query string: parameters for the server.

q: A status code beginning with 4 means:
options: Your request was bad or not allowed
why: By first digit: 2 success, 3 redirect, 4 client error (your request was bad or not allowed, e.g. 404), 5 server error.

q: Which status code means the server itself failed, not your request?
why: 500 Internal Server Error is a 5xx: your request was fine, the server failed. 404 and 403 are 4xx client errors; 301 is a redirect.

q: Where does a GET request carry its parameters, and where does POST carry them?
options: GET in the URL, POST in the body
GET in the body, POST in the URL
why: GET carries parameters in the URL; POST carries them in the body of the message.

q: HTTPS differs from HTTP because it adds:
why: HTTPS = HTTP + TLS encryption and authentication, on port 443. Plain HTTP uses port 80.

q: What is the job of DNS in the request-response cycle?
options: It translates a domain name into an IP address
why: DNS translates a domain name into an IP address so the browser knows which server to contact.

q: A URL ends with #marks. What does the browser do with it?
options: Sends it to the server as a parameter
Scrolls to the element with id='marks'; the fragment is not sent to the server
why: The fragment scrolls to the element with that id. It is handled by the browser and is not sent to the server.

q: What is the difference between a tag and an element?
options: A tag is one bracketed marker; an element is the opening tag, content and closing tag
An element is one marker; a tag is the whole thing
A tag has attributes; an element cannot
why: A tag is one bracketed marker. An element is the opening tag plus content plus the closing tag.

q: Which of these is a void element?
why: Void elements have no content and no closing tag: br, hr, img, input, meta, link, source, track. p, div and textarea are paired.

q: Why is </br> invalid?
options: br is a void element, so it has no closing tag
It works only inside a p
why: br is void: it has no content and therefore no closing tag. Writing </br> is invalid.

q: What happens if you forget to close an HTML comment?
options: The rest of the page is swallowed and does not render
The browser shows an error message
Only the next element is hidden
why: An unclosed comment blanks the rest of the page, because everything after it is treated as comment text.

q: Why must you write &lt; instead of a literal < in page text?
options: A literal < would start a tag
why: A literal < would start a tag, so the entity < is used to display the character itself.

q: In HTML, several spaces and line breaks in a row are:
options: Collapsed to a single space, except inside pre
why: Whitespace collapses to one space everywhere except inside pre, which preserves it.

q: Your page looks fine in the browser but the validator reports errors. What does that tell you?
options: Browsers forgive mistakes and repair markup silently; validators do not
The page will not work on phones
why: Browsers forgive and repair broken markup silently, so a page can look fine and still be invalid. HTML fails silently, which is why you validate.

q: What does <!DOCTYPE html> on line one do?
options: Puts the browser in HTML5 standards mode
why: The doctype selects HTML5 standards mode. Without it the browser falls back to quirks mode.

q: Which of these belongs in the <head>, not the <body>?
why: The head holds invisible metadata: charset, viewport, title, description, link and style. The body holds everything visible.

q: What is the difference between <title> and <h1>?
options: title is the tab text and search headline; h1 is the visible main heading on the page
title is shown at the top of the page
why: title is the tab text, bookmark name and search headline. h1 is the visible main heading in the body.

q: Why is <meta charset='UTF-8'> important?
why: The charset declaration prevents garbled characters by telling the browser how the bytes encode text.

q: Why are scripts usually placed just before </body>?
options: So the content is parsed and displayed first
It is the only legal place
why: Scripts go just before </body> so the content is parsed and displayed before the scripts run.

q: <head> and <header> are:
options: Different: head is invisible metadata, header is a visible introductory region
why: head holds invisible metadata; header is a visible introductory region in the body. They are not the same.

q: What does lang='en' on the <html> element declare?
options: The content language, for screen readers and search engines
why: lang declares the content language for screen readers and search engines. Encoding is set by meta charset.

q: Which global attribute must be unique on the page?
why: id is a unique identifier for one element. class is a reusable group name and an element may carry several.

q: What happens if two elements share the same id?
options: It fails silently: fragment links and scripts find only the first
why: Duplicate ids fail silently. Fragment links and scripts find only the first one.

q: A video has controls='false'. What happens?
options: The controls still show, because controls is a boolean attribute
why: Boolean attributes are on whenever they are present, whatever their value. To hide the controls you remove the attribute.

q: Which attribute points to an embedded resource rather than a link destination?
why: href is for link destinations; src is for embedded resources such as images, scripts and media.

q: Which list contains only inline elements?
why: span, a, strong, em and img are inline: they flow within a line. div, p, section, ul and h1 are block elements.

q: You need a container purely so CSS can style two columns. Which element is correct?
why: div and span are meaningless containers, used exactly when no semantic element fits. section and article carry meaning.

q: What are data-* attributes for?
options: Custom data for scripts, named as you like after data-
why: data-* attributes hold custom data for scripts, named freely after the data- prefix.

q: What is the difference between <strong> and <b>?
options: strong carries strong importance; b draws attention with no extra importance
strong is inline, b is block
why: strong is logical: strong importance, seriousness or urgency. b is physical: draw attention, bold with no extra importance.

q: Which element preserves the whitespace exactly as typed?
why: pre preserves whitespace. Everywhere else it collapses to a single space.

q:
Why should you not use

to create space between paragraphs?
options: br is a line break within one block; spacing is CSS's job, and two paragraphs should be two p elements
It breaks screen readers only in Chrome
why: br is for a line break within one block, such as an address or a poem. Never use br br for spacing.

q: Which element marks a keyboard key the user should press?
why: kbd is keyboard input by the user. code is inline code, samp is sample output, var is a variable.

q: The <cite> element marks:
why: The cite element marks the title of a work. The cite attribute on q or blockquote holds the source URL.

q: Which of these is obsolete and should be replaced?
why: strike, font, center, big, tt and marquee are obsolete. Use del for removed content, or CSS.

q: Headings h1 to h6 should be chosen by:
options: The size you want the text
The level in the document outline, with no skipped levels
why: Headings build an outline: one h1, no skipped levels. Sizes are set in CSS, not by choosing a heading level.

q: Which element may sit directly inside <ul>?
why: Only li may sit directly inside ul or ol. Anything else must go inside an li.

q: You need a list where the order matters. Which element?
why: ul is for lists where order does not matter; ol is for lists where order or rank matters; dl pairs terms with descriptions.

q: <ol type='i'> produces:
why: type='i' gives lowercase Roman numerals. type='I' gives uppercase, type='a' lowercase letters, type='1' decimals.

q: What does the reversed attribute on <ol> do?
options: Counts the numbers downwards while the items stay in source order
why: reversed counts downwards (3, 2, 1). The items stay in source order on screen; only the numbers descend.

q: Where does a nested list go?
options: Inside the li it belongs to, before that li closes
Inside the ul but outside any li
why: A nested list goes inside the li it belongs to, before that li closes.

q: Why is a navigation menu marked up as a list of links inside <nav>?
options: So screen readers announce the item count
Because links must be in lists
why: Menus are lists of links inside nav, so screen readers announce how many items there are. The bullets are removed with CSS.

q: In a description list, which element holds the description?
why: dl holds terms in dt and their descriptions in dd.

q: What does the relative URL ../images/logo.png mean?
options: Go up one folder, then into images
why: ../ moves to the parent folder. A leading / means the site root; a bare name means the same folder.

q: Which attribute supplies the text alternative for an image?
why: alt gives the text alternative. src gives the location of the file.

q: A purely decorative image should have:
why: A decorative image takes alt='': empty but present, so a screen reader skips it silently. Omitting the attribute is wrong.

q: A printer icon is used as a button that prints the page. What should its alt be?
why: A functional image describes the action, not the picture: alt='Print'.

q: Why add rel='noopener noreferrer' to a target='_blank' link?
options: To protect against the new page gaining access to yours, for untrusted sites
why: target='_blank' opens a new tab; rel='noopener noreferrer' is added for untrusted sites as a safety measure.

q: Why set width and height on an ?
options: To stop the layout jumping as the image loads
why: width and height reserve the space, which stops layout jumps as the image loads.

q: Which element pairs an illustration with a caption?
why: figure with figcaption marks a captioned illustration. picture with source and an img fallback chooses between conditional sources.

q: Good link text should:
why: Link text describes the destination, never 'click here'.

q: Why does SVG stay sharp at any size?
options: It stores instructions rather than pixels
why: SVG = Scalable Vector Graphics: it stores drawing instructions, not pixels, so it is sharp at any size.

q: In an SVG, what does viewBox define?
options: The coordinate grid the shapes are drawn on
why: width and height are the rendered size; viewBox is the coordinate grid, with the origin at the top-left and y increasing downward.

q: With viewBox='0 0 200 100' and width='400', a <rect width='100'> appears how wide?
why: The 200-unit grid is drawn 400px wide, so each unit is 2px and a 100-unit rect appears 200 pixels wide.

q: A shape drawn outside the viewBox range is:
why: Anything outside the viewBox is clipped and not drawn. There is no error and no automatic scaling.

q: Which SVG element is closed automatically back to its first point?
why: polygon closes automatically back to the first point; polyline stays open.

q: Why is <line> sometimes invisible?
options: It needs a stroke; the default stroke is none
Lines cannot be seen in SVG
why: fill colours the inside; stroke draws the outline. A line has no interior, so without a stroke it is invisible.

q: In a path's d attribute, what does M do?
why: In a path: M move, L line, H horizontal, V vertical, Q curve, Z close. Lowercase letters are relative.

q: How do you give an inline SVG an accessible name?
why: Inline SVG takes role='img' plus aria-label. SVG has no alt attribute.

q: Which attribute shows the native play/pause/volume UI on a video?
why: controls shows the native player UI. It is boolean: controls='false' still shows them.

q: Why does autoplay often not work?
options: Browsers block it unless the video is also muted
why: autoplay is blocked by browsers unless the video is also muted.

q: What does the poster attribute supply?
options: The image shown before playback begins
why: poster is the image shown before playback begins. It is not a subtitle and not autoplay.

q: Why include several <source> elements inside a <video>?
options: As a fallback chain: the browser plays the first format it supports
why: Several source elements form a fallback chain; the browser plays the first format it supports. mp4 plus webm covers everyone.

q: Which element supplies subtitles or captions?
why: track with src, kind, srclang and label supplies subtitles and captions from a .vtt file.

q: Every <iframe> should carry a title attribute because:
options: Without it a screen reader announces only 'frame'
why: The title gives the embedded content an accessible name. Without it a screen reader announces only 'frame'.

q: What does the sandbox attribute on an iframe do?
options: Removes capabilities, which you then restore individually
why: sandbox removes capabilities; you add allow-scripts or allow-forms to restore them. allow grants capabilities such as fullscreen or camera.

q: Do <audio> and <video> take an alt attribute?
options: No: fallback text goes between the opening and closing tags
why: audio and video are paired elements with no alt attribute. Fallback text goes between the tags.

q: What are the four stages of how a search engine works?
why: Crawl, index, rank, click. Links get you crawled, clear HTML gets you understood, quality and speed get you ranked, title and description win the click.

q: What appears as the clickable headline in a search result?
why: title is the clickable headline in results and the tab text. The meta description is the grey summary underneath.

q: Has the meta keywords tag had SEO value in recent years?
options: Yes, it is the main signal
No, Google has ignored it since 2009
why: Google has ignored the keywords meta tag since 2009. It has no SEO value today.

q: What does robots.txt do?
options: Publicly requests that crawlers skip certain paths
why: robots.txt is a public, advisory file at the site root listing paths crawlers should skip. sitemap.xml lists pages to index.

q: Which tag keeps a single page out of the search index?
why: meta robots noindex keeps that page out of the index.

q: A page repeats 'web development' fifty times in white text on white. What happens?
options: Search engines treat it as manipulation and lower or remove the page
why: Keyword stuffing and hidden text are treated as manipulation. The page is lowered or removed; it does not simply fail validation.

q: Why do SEO and accessibility overlap so much?
options: Both depend on clear structure, alt text, headings and descriptive link text
Both are set in the head
why: The same signals serve both: semantic landmarks, one h1 and a logical outline, alt text and link text that names the destination.

q: Which is the correct house style for HTML?
why: Lowercase element and attribute names, and every attribute value quoted.

q: Writing <div class=my box> breaks because:
options: The unquoted value splits into two attributes
why: An unquoted value ends at the space, so it splits into two attributes. Quote every attribute value.

q: Separation of concerns means:
options: Content in HTML, CSS in an external stylesheet, JavaScript in external files
why: Content goes in HTML, all CSS in an external stylesheet via link, and all JS in external files loaded before </body>.

q: When should you use <a> rather than <button>?
options: When the user is going somewhere; button is for doing something
why: a is for going somewhere, button is for doing something.

q: Which of these was removed in HTML5?
why: frameset and frame were removed in HTML5. Use iframe for embeds and CSS for layout.

q: Why are tables not used for page layout?
options: They break accessibility and responsiveness; tables are for tabular data
why: Layout tables break accessibility and responsiveness. Tables are for tabular data; layout is CSS Flexbox and Grid.

q: Before publishing, which check finds silent HTML mistakes?
options: Running it through the W3C validator
why: HTML fails silently, so you validate at validator.w3.org, then test on a phone with DevTools and check relative paths.

q: What do semantic elements give you that a styled <div> does not?
options: Landmarks for screen readers and a map for search engines
why: Semantic elements render like divs but describe meaning, giving screen readers landmarks and search engines a map of the page.

q: How many <main> elements may a page have?
why: There is one main per page, and it is never nested inside article, aside, header, footer or nav.

q: A blog post that would still make sense republished on another site should be:
why: Use article if the content makes sense elsewhere; section for a themed group with a heading; aside for related but dispensable content.

q: A 'Related articles' sidebar is marked up as:
why: aside is related but non-essential content.

q: Which is true of <footer>?
options: It may appear only once, at the end of the page
It holds closing information and may also sit inside an article
why: footer holds closing information and may sit inside an article as well as at the end of the page.

q: Which element groups navigation links?
why: nav marks a group of navigation links; there is one per group of links.

q: When is <div> the right choice?
options: When there is no meaning to convey and it exists only for CSS
why: div carries no meaning; use it only when no semantic element fits, for example a wrapper that exists only so CSS can style two columns.

q: Why must the HTML read correctly with no CSS at all?
options: HTML supplies structure and CSS only arranges it later; the source order is the real order
why: HTML supplies structure; CSS later arranges it for each screen. The source must read correctly with no CSS at all.

q: In a typical page, the direct children of <body> are:
why: body holds header, nav, main and footer; main then holds the sections, articles and aside.

q: How many <h1> elements should a page normally have?
why: One h1 in the header, then h2 per section and h3 per article.

q: A wireframe shows a narrow 'related links' column beside the content. Which element?
why: A narrow related column maps to aside, placed inside main.

q: Which of these is a layout mistake to unlearn?
options: Laying out with tables, br stacks or fixed widths
why: Do not lay out with tables, br stacks, styled divs or fixed widths.

q: May a <section> contain its own header and footer?
options: Only if it has no heading
why: Sections and articles may carry their own header and footer. What you may never have is a second main.

q: Why is a placeholder not a substitute for a label?
options: It disappears as soon as the user types, and may be skipped by screen readers
why: Placeholder is not a label: it disappears on typing and may be skipped.

q: What joins a <label> to its input?
why: label for must match the input's id, or the label may wrap the control.

q: What is the first rule of ARIA?
options: Prefer the native element; use ARIA only to fill a gap
why: The first rule of ARIA is to prefer the native element. ARIA changes what is announced, never how the element behaves.

q: What does tabindex='-1' do?
options: Puts the element first in the tab order
Removes it from the tab order but allows script focus
Adds it to the tab order
why: tabindex 0 adds an element to the tab order; -1 removes it from the tab order but still allows scripts to focus it.

q: An icon-only close button shows only an x. How do you name it?
why: aria-label gives an element an accessible name when it has no visible text.

q: What is a skip link for?
options: Letting keyboard users bypass the menu and jump to the content
why: Everything must work with Tab, Enter and Space, and a skip link lets keyboard users bypass the menu.

q: Why must colour never be the only signal?
options: Colours look different on each monitor
Colour-blind users cannot tell the states apart
why: Colour plus another cue, such as an icon or text, because colour-blind users cannot tell red from green.

q: Which attribute decides where a form's data is sent?
why: action is where the data goes; method is how (get puts it in the URL, post in the body).

q: A field's value never arrives at the server. What is the most likely cause?
why: name is the submission key: a control without a name is not submitted at all. That is the commonest reason a field goes missing.

q: Which of these is NOT submitted with the form?
why: Disabled controls and unchecked checkboxes are not submitted. readonly fields are submitted.

q: When must a form use method='post'?
options: When it changes data, carries secrets or uploads files
Only when there is no action
why: get puts data in the URL and suits searches; post puts it in the body and suits changes, secrets and files.

q: Which enctype is required to upload a file?
why: enctype='multipart/form-data' is required for uploads.

q: What does <button> do if you write no type attribute?
options: It submits the form, because submit is the default type
why: submit is the default button type. type='button' does nothing on its own; type='reset' clears the form.

q: Which pair groups related controls and captions the group?
why: fieldset groups related controls and legend captions the group.

q: The user must pick exactly one of three options. Which control?
options: A radio group sharing one name
why: Radio buttons are for one of a few choices; they form a group by sharing one name.

q: Which input type masks what the user types?
why: password masks the typed characters as dots. hidden is not displayed at all.

q: Why use type='tel' rather than type='number' for a phone number?
options: number would strip leading zeros and add a spinner
why: tel shows a numeric keypad on phones and does not validate format. number would strip leading zeros and add a spinner.

q: What makes a group of radio buttons one group?
why: Radios form a group by sharing a name; different names make separate groups.

q: Which attribute pre-selects a checkbox or a radio button?
why: checked pre-selects a checkbox or radio. selected is the equivalent on an option inside a select.

q: What does the accept attribute do on <input type='file'>?
options: Suggests which file types to offer
why: accept narrows the file types offered; multiple allows more than one file.

q: Which pair limits the number of characters, not the value?
why: min/max/step constrain the value; minlength/maxlength constrain the character count; size is the visible width.

q: What does the size attribute control on an input?
options: The visible width of the box
why: size is the visible width of the control, not a limit on what can be typed.

q: You want a date of birth with a native calendar. Which type?
why: date gives a native calendar picker. datetime-local adds a time, month picks a month and year.

q: Why is client-side validation never enough on its own?
options: It can be bypassed; server-side validation is the final line of defence
It does not work on phones
why: Client-side validation gives instant feedback but can be bypassed. Server-side validation cannot be, so you use both.

q: Does a placeholder satisfy the required constraint?
options: No: a placeholder is only a hint and the field is still empty
why: A placeholder never satisfies required. The field is still empty.

q: A required <select> always passes validation even when untouched. Why?
options: Its first option has a value, so something is always selected
why: A required select needs an empty first option; otherwise the first real option is already selected and the constraint always passes.

q: Which attribute supplies the hint shown when a pattern fails?
why: pattern is the regular expression and title is the failure hint.

q: How much of the value must match a pattern?
why: The whole value must match the regular expression.

q: Which attribute turns built-in validation off for one button, such as 'Save draft'?
why: novalidate on the form and formnovalidate on a submit button switch built-in validation off deliberately.

q: When a form is submitted with an invalid field, the browser:
options: Blocks submission, focuses the first bad field and shows a message
why: The browser blocks invalid forms, focuses the first bad field and shows a message. :valid and :invalid let you style them.

q: Are disabled fields validated?
options: No: they are neither validated nor submitted
why: Disabled fields are neither validated nor submitted.

q: What is the correct order of children inside <table>?
why: Order inside table: caption, colgroup, thead, tbody, tfoot. The caption is the first child.

q: What is the difference between <th> and <td>?
options: th is a header cell for a column or row; td is a data cell
why: th is a header cell, td is a data cell. Both live inside a tr.

q: A row in a four-column table has a cell with colspan='3'. How many more cells does that row need?
why: The row must still add up to four columns, so one more cell is needed.

q: In the row beneath a cell with rowspan='2', what happens?
options: It omits that cell, because the cell above occupies the space
why: The row under a rowspan cell omits that cell; the cell above already occupies the space.

q: Which attribute tells a screen reader that a <th> heads a row rather than a column?
why: scope='col' or scope='row' on th, plus headers='ids' on td for complex tables, is how screen readers read tables.

q: What is <caption> for?
options: The table's title, written as its first child
why: caption is the table's title and the first child of table.

q: Which pair sets properties for whole columns?
why: colgroup and col style whole columns.

q: When is a table the right element?
why: Tables are for tabular data only. Never lay out a page with a table.

q: What does WCAG stand for?
why: WCAG = Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, published by the W3C's Web Accessibility Initiative. Version 2.2 (2023) is current.

q: What do the four letters of POUR stand for?
why: POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.

q: Which conformance level do most organisations and laws require?
why: Level AA is the target most organisations and laws require. The levels are cumulative: AA includes A.

q: What is the minimum contrast ratio for normal text at level AA?
why: AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. AAA raises these to 7:1 and 4.5:1.

q: What is the minimum contrast for icons, form borders and focus indicators?
why: Non-text contrast (WCAG 2.1) requires 3:1 for icons, form borders and focus indicators.

q: Why is AAA not required for whole sites?
options: Some content simply cannot meet it
why: AAA is the highest level and is not required for whole sites because some content cannot meet it.

q: Which Indian law requires public-facing ICT, including websites, to be accessible?
options: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016
why: In India the RPwD Act 2016 and the GIGW guidelines apply; Section 508 and the ADA are United States instruments.

q: Which testing method would find a control that cannot be reached by keyboard?
options: Navigating the page with the keyboard only
why: Test with an automated tool, then keyboard only, a screen reader, zoom and contrast, and validation. Only keyboard testing finds unreachable controls.

q: What does 'responsive' mean?
options: One document that adapts, using HTML structure, CSS media queries and scalable media
why: Responsive means one document that adapts: HTML structure plus CSS media queries plus scalable media.

q: What is the correct viewport meta tag?
why: width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0 gives the real width and 100% zoom. Without it phones show a shrunken desktop layout.

q: A section has a fixed pixel height. What breaks on a phone?
options: The text overflows when it wraps onto more lines
why: Fixed pixel heights break because text wraps onto more lines on a narrow screen and overflows. Let height come from the content.

q: Which CSS declaration stops images overflowing their container?
why: max-width: 100% lets media scale down with the container without stretching beyond its natural size.

q: A page scrolls sideways on a phone. Which habit is the most likely cause?
options: A fixed pixel width on a container
why: Fixed pixel widths on containers are wider than the phone and force sideways scrolling. Use fluid widths or max-widths.

q: How should a wide table behave on a phone?
options: Shrink its font until it fits
why: Wide tables scroll inside a wrapper rather than forcing the whole page to scroll.

q: Why does logical source order matter for responsive pages?
options: It gives a correct single-column view for free
why: Logical source order gives a correct single-column view for free, before any CSS is applied.

q: In the rule h1 { color: navy; font-size: 2rem; }, how many declarations are there?
why: A declaration is one property-value pair ending in a semicolon. There are two here: color: navy and font-size: 2rem.

q: Which way of adding CSS should a real project use?
options: A style attribute on each element
An external stylesheet linked with <link rel='stylesheet'>
why: An external stylesheet keeps one file styling every page, so a single change updates the whole site.

q: What is the correct syntax for a CSS comment?
why: CSS comments are /* ... */. The <!-- --> form is HTML and // is JavaScript.

q: Your rule appears in DevTools but is crossed out. What does that mean?
options: Another rule won the cascade and overrode it
why: A crossed-out rule was matched but overridden. If the rule were not listed at all, the selector matched nothing.

q: What does CSS stand for?
why: CSS = Cascading Style Sheets. 'Cascading' names the rules that decide which declaration wins.

q: In p { color: red; }, which part is the selector?
why: The selector chooses the elements (p); the declaration block in braces says what to do to them.

q: Why is CSS kept separate from HTML?
options: HTML carries meaning and CSS carries appearance, so each can change without the other
It reduces the number of files
why: HTML carries meaning, CSS carries appearance. Separating them lets you restyle a whole site without touching the content.

q: Which selector targets class='card'?
why: A full stop selects a class; a hash selects an id; a bare name selects an element type.

q: What does the universal selector * match?
options: Nothing until you add a class
why: * matches every element. It is often used to apply box-sizing: border-box to the whole page.

q: When two selectors have the same specificity, which rule wins?
options: The one written later in the stylesheet
why: Source order is the tie-breaker. With equal specificity the later rule wins.

q: When does source order decide the winner?
options: Only when the specificity scores are equal
why: Source order is the tie-breaker: it decides only when specificity is equal. The later rule wins.

q: Which selector selects only direct children?
why: > selects direct children only; a space selects any descendant; + is the next sibling and ~ all later siblings.

q: Which group of properties is inherited by children?
why: Text properties such as color, font-family and line-height inherit. Box properties such as padding, border, margin and width do not.

q: Why is !important discouraged?
options: It overrides the cascade, so the only way to beat it later is another !important
It works in one browser only
why: !important short-circuits the cascade. Once used, the only way to override it is another !important, which escalates quickly.

q: What does #FF0000 represent?
why: A hex colour is #RRGGBB. FF is the maximum for red, 00 for green and blue, so #FF0000 is pure red.

q: What does the fourth value in rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.5) control?
why: The fourth value in rgba() is alpha: the opacity, from 0 (transparent) to 1 (opaque).

q: In hsl(), what are the three values in order?
why: hsl() takes hue in degrees, saturation as a percentage and lightness as a percentage.

q: Which property stops a background image repeating?
why: background-repeat: no-repeat stops the tiling. Backgrounds tile by default.

q: Why must you check colour contrast before shipping a colour pair?
options: Because text below the contrast minimum is unreadable for many users and fails WCAG AA
why: WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text. A pair that looks fine to you can be unreadable for others.

q: Does padding take the element's background colour?
options: Yes: the background fills the content and the padding
Only if a border is set
why: The background colour fills the content and the padding, right out to the border. The margin stays transparent.

q: Which of these is an absolute unit?
why: px is absolute. em, rem and % are all relative to something else.

q: What does height: 100vh give an element?
options: The full height of the page
The full height of the viewport
why: vh is a percentage of the viewport height, so 100vh is exactly the height of the visible window.

q: Why can nested em font sizes compound unexpectedly?
options: Each level is relative to its parent's computed size, so they multiply
why: em is relative to the element's inherited font size, so nesting multiplies the factor at each level. rem avoids this by always referring to the root.

q: The unit ch is measured as:
options: The width of the digit zero in the current font
why: 1ch is the width of the '0' character in the current font, which makes it useful for setting readable line lengths.

q: A percentage width is measured against:
why: A percentage is a share of the containing block, which is why a percentage width needs a parent with a known width.

q: What is a font stack and why does it end with a generic family?
options: A list of sizes; the last is the default
A list of fallbacks; the generic family guarantees something readable renders
why: font-family lists fallbacks in order. Ending with a generic family such as sans-serif guarantees a readable result if none of the named fonts exist.

q: Which value makes text bold?
why: font-weight controls boldness; 400 is normal and 700 is bold. font-style controls italics.

q: A unitless line-height such as 1.5 is preferred because:
options: It scales with each element's own font size instead of being inherited as a fixed length
It is the only valid form
why: A unitless line-height is inherited as a ratio, so every element computes it from its own font size.

q: Which is true of the font shorthand?
options: font-size and font-family are required and must come last, in that order
why: The font shorthand has a required order ending in font-size and font-family; omitting either makes the declaration invalid.

q: How many typefaces should a typical page use?
why: Pick two, never five: usually one for headings and one for body text.

q: Which property centres a line of text inside its box?
why: text-align: center centres the inline content inside the box. margin: 0 auto centres the box itself.

q: Why is text-align: justify used carefully in narrow columns?
options: The extra word spacing forms distracting vertical rivers of white
why: Justify straightens the right edge by stretching the spaces between words; in a narrow column those gaps line up into rivers.

q: Which property removes the underline from a link?
why: text-decoration: none removes the underline. Remember to leave another cue so links stay identifiable.

q: text-transform: uppercase changes:
options: The text in the HTML source
Only how the text is displayed
why: text-transform changes only the presentation. The underlying text in the HTML is unchanged, which matters for screen readers and copy-paste.

q: In text-shadow: 2px 4px 6px grey, what is 6px?
why: text-shadow takes horizontal offset, vertical offset, blur radius, then colour.

q: Which layer is the space INSIDE the border?
why: From the inside out: content, padding, border, margin. Padding is inside the border; margin is outside it.

q: width: 200px, padding: 20px, border: 5px, with no box-sizing. How wide is the box on screen?
why: By default width sizes the content only: 5 + 20 + 200 + 20 + 5 = 250px.

q: Which layer of the box model is always transparent?
why: The background fills the content and the padding out to the border. The margin is always transparent.

q: In 'padding: 10px 20px 30px', what does 20px apply to?
why: With three values the order is top, then left-and-right, then bottom.

q: Which layer sits between the padding and the margin?
why: From the inside out: content, padding, border, margin. The border is the visible edge between padding and margin.

q: Which pair of margins can collapse into one?
options: Left and right margins of neighbours
The vertical margins of stacked block elements
why: Vertical margins between stacked block elements collapse into the larger of the two rather than adding up.

q: How do you horizontally centre a block that has a set width?
why: margin: 0 auto shares the leftover horizontal space equally, which centres the box. There is no float: center.

q: What is the default value of position?
why: Every element is position: static until you say otherwise, and offsets are ignored on a static box.

q: Which position moves an element but keeps its original space in the flow?
why: relative offsets the element visually while its original space stays reserved. absolute and fixed remove it from the flow.

q: An absolutely positioned box flies to the corner of the page. What is missing?
options: A positioned ancestor, so it is using the page as its reference
why: An absolute box is placed against its nearest positioned ancestor. With none, it falls back to the page.

q: Which position is measured against the viewport, so it stays put when you scroll?
why: fixed is measured against the viewport and does not move when the page scrolls.

q: position: sticky silently does nothing. What is usually missing?
options: A threshold such as top, and a scrollable ancestor that is tall enough
why: Sticky needs an offset such as top: 0 to stick to, and room to scroll within its parent.

q: Why does z-index sometimes appear to do nothing?
options: It applies only to positioned elements, and only within the same stacking context
why: z-index applies only to positioned elements, and it orders siblings within one stacking context.

q: Where do you put display: flex?
why: display: flex goes on the parent. Its direct children become flex items.

q: Which property aligns flex items along the CROSS axis?
why: align-items works along the cross axis; justify-content works along the main axis.

q: What does flex-direction: row-reverse do?
options: Lays the items along the row in the opposite order
Reverses the text in each item
why: row-reverse keeps the main axis horizontal but runs it the other way, so the items appear in reverse order.

q: Which pair centres content both horizontally and vertically in a flex row?
why: In a flex row, justify-content: center centres along the main axis and align-items: center along the cross axis.

q: What does flex: 1 on every item achieve?
options: They share the leftover space equally
why: flex: 1 lets each item take an equal share of the leftover space.

q: By default, do flex items wrap onto a new line?
options: No: they stay on one line until flex-wrap: wrap is set
why: Flex items stay on one line by default and squash to fit. flex-wrap: wrap lets them move onto a new line.

q: What does flex: 0 0 140px mean on an item?
options: Never grow, never shrink, stay 140px wide
why: The three parts are grow, shrink and basis. 0 0 140px means it neither grows nor shrinks from its 140px basis.

q: grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 200px creates how many columns?
why: Each value in grid-template-columns defines one column track, so this is three columns: two fixed and one flexible.

q: What does minmax(200px, 1fr) mean for a grid track?
options: At least 200px, at most one share of the free space
why: minmax sets a floor and a ceiling: never narrower than 200px, and at most one share of the leftover space.

q: Flexbox handles one dimension. Grid handles:
why: Flexbox arranges along one line; Grid defines rows and columns together so things line up in both directions.

q: Which property defines the columns of a grid?
why: grid-template-columns lists the column tracks; grid-template-rows does the same for rows.

q: You need a row of buttons that simply sit in a line. Flex or Grid?
why: Use Flex for a line of things and Grid for a plan with rows and columns.

q: How many colons does a pseudo-CLASS use?
why: A pseudo-class uses one colon (:hover). A pseudo-element uses two (::before).

q: Which pseudo-class matches a form control the user cannot interact with?
why: :disabled matches a disabled control. :checked, :required and :invalid describe other form states.

q: What does li:nth-child(odd) select?
why: odd matches the 1st, 3rd, 5th and so on; even matches the 2nd, 4th, 6th.

q: Which pseudo-class matches a ticked checkbox?
why: :checked matches a checked checkbox or radio; :disabled, :required and :invalid describe other form states.

q: What does :first-child mean?
options: The first element of its type
An element that is the first child of its parent
The first element on the page
why: :first-child matches an element that is the first child of its parent, whatever its type.

q: In the order of link pseudo-classes, which must come last for hover to work?
why: The order is :link, :visited, :hover, :active. Since they have equal specificity, a later rule wins, so hover and active must come after visited.

q: Why do ::before and ::after not work on an ?
options: They insert content inside an element, and a void element has no inside
why: ::before and ::after add a child inside the element. A void element such as img has no content model, so there is nowhere to insert.

q: content: '' together with a width and height is typically used to:
why: An empty content value still creates the box, so you can give it a size and a background and use it as decoration.

q: Where does ::before insert its content?
options: Before the element in the HTML
Inside the element, before its existing content
why: ::before inserts inside the element, before its content. ::after inserts inside, after its content.

q: Content generated by ::before is:
options: Presentational, and not reliably available to assistive technology or copy-paste
Indexed by search engines as body text
why: Generated content is decoration. Anything that carries meaning belongs in the HTML.

q: Which pseudo-element styles the first line of a paragraph?
why: ::first-line styles the first rendered line; ::first-letter styles only the opening character.

q: Which selector matches an element whose class list contains the whole word 'card'?
why: ~= matches one whole word in a space-separated list. *= would also match 'cardboard'.

q: a[href^='https'] selects links whose href:
why: ^= means starts with, $= means ends with, and *= means contains anywhere.

q: Which selector finds links to PDF files?
why: $= matches the end of the value, so a[href$='.pdf'] finds links ending in .pdf.

q: What does [data-state] with no value select?
options: Every element that has a data-state attribute at all
why: An attribute selector with no value matches every element that carries the attribute, whatever its value.

q: Why set font: inherit on form controls?
options: Browsers give controls their own font, so without it they do not match the page
why: Form controls come with a browser font of their own. font: inherit makes them match the rest of the page.

q: Why prefer changing the outline on :focus rather than removing it?
options: Removing it leaves keyboard users with no visible indication of where they are
why: An outline takes up no space and shows keyboard users where they are. Replace it with something visible; never simply remove it.

q: Which does NOT take up space in the layout?
why: An outline is drawn over the layout and takes no space, which is why it suits focus rings.

q: A styled form still needs a real <label> because:
options: The label is announced with the field and clicking it focuses the field
why: Styling is CSS's job, but the label must exist in the HTML: it is announced with the field and clicking it focuses the control.

q: Where must a CSS variable be declared to be available everywhere?
why: :root is the html element, the top of the tree, so custom properties declared there are inherited by everything.

q: Which is a valid custom property declaration?
why: A custom property is declared with two leading hyphens: --brand: navy; and read back with var(--brand).

q: What is the second argument in var(--brand, navy)?
options: A fallback used if --brand is not defined
why: The second argument is a fallback, used when the custom property is missing or invalid.

q: Custom properties differ from Sass variables because they:
options: Are live in the browser and inherit, so they can be changed at runtime
why: Custom properties are real CSS: they inherit down the tree and can be changed at runtime, including from JavaScript.

q: Your media queries are ignored on a phone. What is almost always missing?
why: Without <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0'> the phone pretends to be a wide desktop, so width-based media queries never match.

q: What does @media (max-width: 600px) target?
why: max-width is a ceiling: the rules apply at that width and below. min-width is a floor.

q: What does mobile-first mean in CSS terms?
options: Writing the desktop rules first and overriding them
Writing the base rules for small screens, then adding min-width queries
why: Mobile-first writes the small-screen layout as the base and adds rules with min-width as space allows.

q: Where should a breakpoint be placed?
options: Where the content starts to look wrong
At the width of the newest iPhone
why: Content decides breakpoints: resize slowly and add one where the layout breaks, rather than chasing device sizes.

q: What is the default transition-timing-function?
why: The default is ease: it starts slowly, speeds up and slows down at the end. linear runs at a constant rate.

q: In transition: background-color 0.3s ease, what is 0.3s?
why: The order is property, duration, timing function, then optional delay.

q: Which property pair is cheapest for the browser to animate smoothly?
why: transform and opacity can be handled without re-running layout, so they stay smooth. Animating width, height or margin forces a reflow.

q: Can every CSS property be transitioned?
options: No: only animatable properties, so display cannot be transitioned
why: Only animatable properties transition. display is not one, which is why fading something out usually uses opacity plus visibility.

q: Which animation property decides how the element looks before it starts and after it ends?
why: animation-fill-mode decides whether the first and last keyframe values are held outside the animation's running time.

q: What does animation-iteration-count: infinite do?
options: Runs the animation once very slowly
why: infinite repeats the animation without stopping.

q: Which is the key difference between a transition and an animation?
options: A transition needs a trigger such as :hover; an animation can run on its own and use many keyframes
why: A transition interpolates between two states when something changes. An animation defines its own keyframe sequence and can run without any trigger.

q: Why respect prefers-reduced-motion?
options: Motion can cause nausea and migraine for some users, and WCAG requires a way to avoid it
why: Some users experience nausea or migraine from motion. The media query lets you honour the setting they have already chosen.

q: In @keyframes, what do 'from' and 'to' correspond to?
why: from is 0% and to is 100%. Percentage keyframes let you add steps in between.
